## What Bylda is not

Worth being direct, because the category is crowded and several adjacent products look superficially similar.

Not a CRM. Yours stays the system of record. Bylda reads from it and writes behavioral context back. No migration. See integrations .

Not a call recorder. Recording is an input, and a commoditized one. The product is the finding, not the archive.

Not a dashboard. Dashboards report numbers and leave the interpretation to you. Bylda returns a ranked finding and the change it implies.

Not a chatbot. There is no box to ask questions into and hope. The audit arrives whether or not anyone opens the product.

Not a mood score. Bylda reads tone, emotion and sentiment, but only as signals tied to a moment you can replay, with confidence stated — see what it reads and how .

## How Bylda Works — Trace, Signal, Echo, Directive, Outcome

Source: https://usebylda.com/how-it-works

How It Works

# Trace. Signal. Echo.

Directive. Outcome.

Five stages, each grounded in the one before it. The vocabulary is precise because the steps are genuinely different from one another — and because the last one is what makes the first four honest.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

The homepage shows this loop as Events, Behaviors, Patterns, Outcomes, then Change. Here it is in finer steps: a Trace is the evidence in an event, a Signal is a behavior read in context, an Echo is a pattern, a Directive is the change, and the Outcome is its test.

## Before anything: connect

Bylda reads from the systems your conversations already live in — your CRM, dialer, and call recorder — or from a manual upload. OAuth connection, scoped to what it needs, reviewed before the first read. There is no bot to invite to meetings, nothing for a rep to switch on, and no migration.

Most teams are producing audits within a day of connecting, because the input is conversations that already happened.

Stage 01

## Trace — the evidence.

A Trace is one piece of behavioral evidence detected inside a conversation. Raw, timestamped, and not yet interpreted.

Traces are deliberately atomic. They are facts about a recording — the rep interrupted here, the buyer paused there, price was stated at this second, this question was asked and that one wasn't. On their own they mean very little, which is the point: everything above this layer has to be derived from something checkable.

Traces — Halden Systems, 31:04

RAW

04:18 Buyer asks about rollout timeline

09:12 Price stated by rep

09:41 Buyer objection — "that's higher than we modeled"

09:42 Rep begins response (1.4s latency)

11:13 Rep response ends (91s continuous)

11:13→31:04 Zero buyer questions

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

Signals

INTERPRETED

Risk signal

Price was introduced before any decision criteria were established.

TRACE 09:12 · NO CRITERIA QUESTIONS PRIOR

Behavioral signal

The objection was answered in 1.4 seconds, then held for 91.

TRACES 09:41 → 11:13

Engagement signal

Buyer question rate went to zero and never recovered.

TRACE 11:13 ONWARD

Stage 02

## Signal — what mattered.

A Trace becomes a Signal when context makes it consequential. Same evidence, now interpreted against the shape of the conversation and the state of the deal.

This is where most of the judgment lives. A two-second pause before answering an objection is a Trace; it becomes a Signal only in a conversation where the objection was substantive and the answer that followed was long and unprompted. The same Trace in a different conversation means nothing, and Bylda should say nothing.

Signals come in kinds — risk, buying, coaching, behavioral — and every one carries the Traces it was built from, so a rep can disagree with the interpretation and check the evidence.

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

Stage 03

## Echo — what repeats.

A Signal in one conversation is an anecdote. The same Signal across many conversations is an Echo — and Echoes are the only thing worth changing a process over.

Price before criteria

→ ECHO

9 of this rep's 18 conversations

Objection answered under 2 seconds

→ ECHO

4 reps, concentrated in stalled deals

Signer absent from every call

→ ECHO

Most stalled opportunities this quarter

This is the step that turns call analysis into organizational intelligence. One rep's habit is a coaching conversation. The same habit on four reps is an enablement gap, a hiring profile, or a broken step in your sales process — and you would never find it one call at a time.

Echoes are always grounded in counted, repeated evidence. Nothing here is a vibe.

Stage 04

## Directive — the change.

One specific, executable change. Expressed as an action rather than a quality, ranked so there is only ever one, and carrying the evidence that produced it.

Derived from an Echo, never from a single call

Phrased as something to do on the next call, not a trait to improve

One per rep at a time — behavior change has a throughput limit

Evidence attached, so the rep can disagree and check

How directives work in practice →

Directive

ISSUED

Rep directive

Establish how they decide — and who signs — before you quote a number.

Because

Price preceded criteria in 9 of your last 18 conversations.

HALDEN 09:12 · MERIDIAN 22:40 · NORTHSTAR 14:08

Manager directive

Run one session on decision criteria before pricing. Two reps first.

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

## Stage 05 — Outcome, and why it is the important one

Every stage above is a claim. The Outcome is the only thing that tests them.

Bylda records what happened after the directive: meeting booked or not, deal advanced, stalled, won, lost, renewed, churned. Then it asks the question almost no coaching tool asks about itself — did the reps who changed this behavior actually see different results?

A directive that stops working stops being given. Software that cannot do that is just an opinion with a login.

Over enough cycles the loop produces something specific to you: an account of which behaviors precede revenue in your market, with your buyers, at your price point. That accumulation is the Behavior Graph , and it is the part of Bylda that cannot be bought or copied.

One honest caveat, stated in the product as well as here: observed association is not proof of cause. What the loop supports is a well-evidenced claim worth acting on and re-measuring — not a guarantee. Where the evidence is still thin, Bylda says so rather than inventing confidence.

Questions

## Answered plainly.

What is a Trace in Bylda? +

One piece of behavioral evidence detected inside a sales conversation, timestamped and not yet interpreted — the rep interrupted here, price was stated at this second, this question was asked and that one was not. Traces are deliberately atomic so that everything derived above them remains checkable.

What is a Signal in Bylda? +

A Trace that matters once context is applied. The same evidence interpreted against the shape of the conversation and the state of the deal — for example, that price was introduced before any decision criteria were established. Every Signal carries the Traces it was built from.

What is an Echo in Bylda? +

A Signal that repeats across calls, reps, accounts, or outcomes. One rep's habit is an anecdote; the same behavior on four reps is a system problem. Echoes are always grounded in counted, repeated evidence and are what turn call analysis into organizational intelligence.

What is a Directive in Bylda? +

The specific, executable change Bylda recommends — expressed as an action rather than a quality, derived from an Echo rather than a single call, limited to one per rep at a time, and carrying the evidence that produced it.

Why does the Outcome stage matter? +

Because it is the only thing that tests the other four. Bylda records what happened after a directive was given and asks whether reps who changed the behavior actually saw different results. A directive that stops working stops being given.

## What Is Behavioral Sales Intelligence? | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/behavioral-sales-intelligence

The Category

# Behavioral sales intelligence.

Sales software has spent decades tracking what salespeople do . Behavioral sales intelligence measures how they behave — and connects that behavior to the revenue it produced.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

## The definition

Behavioral sales intelligence is software that analyzes the observable behavior inside sales conversations — questions asked, discovery depth, interruptions, listening ratio, pacing, the order in which pricing and decision criteria come up, who was actually in the room, the language of commitment or resistance — identifies which of those behaviors repeat, and connects them to the outcomes that followed.

The distinction from everything before it is the unit of measurement. Activity metrics count events: calls made, meetings booked, emails sent, stages advanced. Behavioral measurement describes conduct : not that a call happened, but what the seller and buyer actually did during it, in what order, and what happened as a result.

Activity tells you a conversation occurred. Behavior tells you why it worked.

## Why activity metrics stopped being enough

Every sales organization already knows its activity numbers, and almost none of them can answer the question a VP actually cares about: why does one rep close at twice the rate of another rep making the same number of calls?

The answer is always behavioral, and it is almost always specific. One rep confirms decision criteria before demonstrating anything. One answers pricing objections in under two seconds. One asks eleven discovery questions; one asks three and fills the silence with product. None of this appears in a dashboard, because none of it is an event — it is conduct, and conduct had no data type.

## What behavioral sales intelligence measures

Three categories of conduct, each tied to a moment you can replay:

Seller behavior — question quality and frequency, discovery depth and duration, interruptions, listening ratio, pacing, pitch timing, objection handling, framework execution, closing behavior, follow-up quality, and the language patterns the rep reaches for under pressure.

Buyer behavior — questions asked and when they stop, objections raised and repeated, pricing sensitivity, implementation interest, decision-maker presence, commitment language, urgency, and resistance.

Conversation behavior — turning points, where control shifted, the sequence of pricing and criteria, discovery gaps, and the moments a deal was actually decided.

Bylda also reads tone, emotion and sentiment as signals: where a buyer’s sentiment cooled, where a rep’s tone changed. Each is tied to the moment it came from and shown with a confidence level, next to conduct you can verify yourself by listening to the timestamp it cites.

The Phantom Layer

## Where behavioral intelligence lives.

We call it the Phantom Layer: the behavioral stratum beneath the visible pipeline. Always present, never previously recorded.

Visible layer — the record

Structured, reportable, silent on causes.

Stage Amount Activity Owner Loss reason

Where it sits

## Not a recorder. Not a scorecard.

Not a forecast.

How behavioral sales intelligence relates to adjacent categories

Category What it measures What it returns Its limit

CRM Salesforce, HubSpot Activity and record state Reports on what was entered No account of conduct

Conversation intelligence Gong, Chorus What was said on a call Searchable calls and metrics A human still has to review and decide

Revenue intelligence Clari Pipeline aggregates Forecasts and roll-ups Bounded by CRM accuracy

Behavioral sales intelligence Bylda Conduct, repetition, and outcome A directive, and its evidence —

These categories overlap, and good products exist in each. The difference is architectural: behavior as the unit of measurement, a directive as the output, and the outcome as the test.

For the sharper version of the comparison closest to us, see conversation intelligence vs behavioral intelligence →

## How Bylda implements it

Five stages, each grounded in the one before it. The vocabulary is proprietary because the steps are:

Trace — one piece of behavioral evidence inside a conversation.

Signal — a trace that matters, once context is applied.

Echo — a signal that repeats across calls, reps, accounts, or outcomes.

Directive — the specific change worth making, with its evidence.

Outcome — what followed, and the only honest test of the directive.

Run continuously, that sequence is the Phantom Audit . Accumulated over time, it becomes the Behavior Graph — the record of which behaviors produce revenue in your company specifically.

## Why the CRM stays

Behavioral sales intelligence is not a system of record and should not try to be. Your CRM holds the deal; Bylda holds the explanation. It reads from the CRM for context and never asks anyone to migrate anything.

FAQ

## Behavioral sales intelligence, answered.

What is behavioral sales intelligence? +

Software that analyzes the observable behavior inside sales conversations — questions asked, discovery depth, interruptions, listening ratio, pacing, the order in which pricing and decision criteria come up, who was in the room, the language of commitment or resistance — identifies which behaviors repeat, and connects them to the outcomes that followed. Where activity metrics count events, behavioral intelligence describes conduct.

How is it different from conversation intelligence? +

Conversation intelligence makes calls searchable and reports metrics about them; a human still has to review the output and decide what to do. Behavioral sales intelligence treats a single call as one sample, looks for the behaviors that repeat across the whole team, and returns a specific directive with the evidence for it — then checks that directive against what actually happened next.

What behaviors can actually be measured? +

Conduct and the signals around it: question count and quality, discovery duration and depth, interruptions, listening ratio, speaking pace, response latency after an objection, pitch and pricing timing relative to discovery, framework execution, who attended, commitment or resistance language, and tone, emotion and sentiment. Each reading is tied to a moment you can replay and carries a confidence level.

Does it replace the CRM? +

No. The CRM remains the system of record. Bylda is the system of intelligence on top of it: it reads CRM context, adds behavioral context back, and requires no migration.

Is this just AI call scoring? +

No. A score is a number without a reason, and it does not change behavior. Bylda's output is a directive — one specific change, with the moment that justifies it — and the outcome that follows is used to judge whether the directive was right.

## AI Sales Call Auditing — The Phantom Audit | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/sales-call-auditing

The Phantom Audit

# Every conversation becomes evidence.

Bylda audits every sales call your team has — continuously, not on request — and returns what worked, what cost you, what is repeating, and the one change worth making. No call review required.

Request access →

For managers

## Why sales call auditing is broken

The standard process is a manager listening to calls. It is the right instinct and it does not scale: a manager with eight reps has roughly three hundred conversations a week and time for maybe five. Whatever is going wrong at scale is happening in the 295 nobody hears.

The tools built to help mostly moved the problem. Recording made calls searchable, which means a manager can now find the call they still do not have time to listen to. Scorecards produced a number without a reason. Both leave the actual work — noticing the pattern, deciding what to coach — exactly where it was.

Searchable calls are not reviewed calls. Somebody still has to do the listening, and nobody has the hours.

## What an audit is instead

A Phantom Audit is not a recording, a transcript, a summary, or a score. It is a finding: a claim about behavior, the evidence behind it, and the change it implies. Short enough to read before a first meeting.

Anatomy

## Five findings, ranked.

Hierarchy is the whole design. A rep does not need forty metrics; they need to know the one thing to change before their next call.

Strongest behavior — what to repeat deliberately

Biggest leak — what cost you, with the timestamp

Top echo — the pattern repeating across conversations

Directive — the specific change, and why

Evidence — every claim traceable to a moment you can verify

At team scale

## One rep's habit is a note.

Four reps' habit is a system problem.

The same audit runs across the organization, and that is where it stops being a coaching tool and becomes intelligence.

When a behavior shows up on one rep's calls, it is worth a conversation. When it shows up on four, it is a hiring profile, an enablement gap, or a broken part of your sales process — and you would never have found it one call at a time.

Echoes ranked by how often they appear and where they concentrate

Revenue leaks located in the conversation, not inferred from the pipeline

Top-performer behavior made explicit, so it can be taught

Rep-to-rep differences described as conduct, not ranked on a leaderboard

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

FAQ

## Sales call auditing, answered.

What is a sales call audit? +

A structured review of what actually happened in a sales conversation — the questions asked, the discovery done, how objections were handled, the order pricing and criteria came up, who attended — and what that implies about the outcome. Traditionally a manager does this by listening. Bylda does it on every call automatically and returns the findings ranked.

How do you audit sales calls at scale? +

Not by reviewing more of them manually — the arithmetic never works. The approach that scales is to analyze every conversation for observable behaviors, look for the behaviors that repeat across reps and outcomes, and surface only the small number of findings that are both recurring and consequential. A manager then reviews findings rather than recordings.

Is this the same as call scoring? +

No. A score compresses a conversation into a number and discards the reason, which is the only part a rep can act on. A Phantom Audit returns a claim about behavior, the moment that evidences it, and the change it implies. Where scores appear at all, they are secondary to the finding.

Do managers still need to listen to calls? +

Far fewer, and for a different purpose. Bylda tells you which moment matters and why, so listening becomes verification of a specific timestamp rather than a search through a recording. Most managers keep listening to a handful of calls a week — by choice, not obligation.

Does it feel like surveillance to reps? +

That depends entirely on design, and we have made deliberate choices: the rep sees their own audit first, findings are framed as conduct rather than character, strengths are reported alongside leaks, and there is no leaderboard. Bylda is built to be the most useful thing in a rep's morning, not a stick for their manager.

## AI Sales Call Analysis — Structure, Not Transcripts | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/ai-sales-call-analysis

AI Sales Call Analysis

# What one call actually tells you.

A transcript is a record of words. Bylda reads a conversation the way an experienced manager does — the questions, the order, the pauses, who held control — and turns it into findings you can act on.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

## Transcription is not analysis

Accurate transcription has been a commodity for years. Every vendor has roughly the same word error rate, and none of it answers a manager's question, because the interesting information in a sales call is not the words — it is the structure.

Who asked the questions. How many, and how open. Whether discovery happened before the pitch or after it. How long the rep waited before answering an objection, and how long they talked once they started. Which moment the buyer stopped asking questions. Whether the person who signs was even in the room.

Two calls can contain nearly identical words and mean opposite things. The difference is in the order and the timing.

## From conversation to finding

Bylda works in stages, and the vocabulary is precise because the stages are distinct.

01

Trace

Raw behavioral evidence, timestamped.

09:12 — price stated. No decision questions asked before this point.

02

Signal

The traces that mattered to this conversation.

Buyer asked six questions before pricing, none after.

03

Echo

Whether this call repeats a wider pattern.

Same sequence in half of this rep's recent conversations.

04

Directive

The change worth making next time.

Ask how they decide before you quote.

05

Outcome

What followed — the test of all of the above.

No second meeting booked.

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

Worked example

## The same three minutes, read two ways.

A transcript search for "too expensive" finds the objection. It cannot tell you that the objection was invited, or that the response made it worse.

Bylda reads the sequence: the price landed before any decision criteria were established, the buyer's question rate dropped to zero immediately afterward, and the rep filled the gap with 90 seconds of unprompted justification. Three observations, each verifiable, that together explain an outcome the CRM recorded as "Lost — Price."

Discovery duration and what it covered

Response latency after each objection

Talk-time distribution, and where it shifted

Attendance — who was actually on the call

Turning points, with timestamps

Boundaries

## What Bylda reads, and how it holds itself to it.

Call-analysis products often imply they know how people felt, then ask you to take it on trust. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment, and holds those scores to the same standard as everything else on this site.

Every reading is tied to a moment you can replay: the words and the delivery at that timestamp, with a confidence level beside it. A shift in sentiment is shown on the call timeline next to what happened just before it, so you can see what moved it.

Bylda reports these as signals about a conversation, not verdicts about a person . A rise in frustration at 18:42 is something to listen to and ask about, not a rating of the buyer or the rep. Readings from voice and language are probabilistic, so each carries its confidence, and a reading with too little evidence is flagged rather than shown. Bylda does not type personalities.

FAQ

## Sales call analysis, answered.

How do you analyze a sales call? +

Start with structure rather than words: count and classify the questions each side asked, measure how long discovery ran and what it covered, note where pricing landed relative to decision criteria, measure how quickly the rep responded to each objection and how long they then talked, check who actually attended, and mark the point where buyer engagement and sentiment changed. Those observations explain outcomes; a word-level transcript does not.

What should you look for in a lost-deal call? +

Three things first. Whether discovery preceded the pitch. Whether the person who signs was ever present. And whether the stated loss reason matches the conversation — "lost on price" very often turns out to be a deal where price arrived before value or criteria were established, which is a sequencing problem rather than a pricing one.

Is AI call analysis just transcription plus keywords? +

Keyword search tells you a topic came up. It cannot tell you the topic came up in the wrong order, or that the response to it doubled the rep's talk time. The information in a sales call is largely structural — sequence, timing, distribution — and that is what Bylda measures.

Does Bylda detect tone and emotion? +

Yes. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment alongside observable delivery such as speaking pace, pauses, interruptions and response latency. Each reading is tied to the moment it came from, so you can replay it, and carries a confidence level. Treat it as a signal to investigate, not a verdict on a person.

## AI Sales Coaching That Names One Thing | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/ai-sales-coaching

AI Sales Coaching

# Coaching that names one thing.

Most sales coaching fails for a boring reason: it arrives late, it is based on whichever call a manager happened to hear, and it asks a rep to change five things at once. Bylda gives one directive, from the rep's own conversations, with the moment that justifies it.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

## Why generic AI coaching does not change behavior

Point a language model at a transcript and it will produce plausible advice: ask more open questions, build rapport, confirm next steps. All true, all useless — because the rep already knows it, it is not specific to what they did, and there is no evidence attached that would make them believe it applies to them.

Coaching changes behavior when three things are true at once. It is specific enough to execute on the next call. It is grounded in something the rep actually did, that they can go and verify. And there is exactly one of it.

A rep given five things to fix will fix none of them. That is not a discipline problem, it is a working-memory problem.

## What a Directive is

Bylda's coaching output is a Directive : the single change most likely to matter, expressed as an action rather than a quality.

Not "improve your objection handling." Instead: "Pause two seconds after a pricing objection, then ask one question before you answer."

Not "do better discovery." Instead: "Establish how they decide, and who signs, before you quote a number."

Not "build more urgency." Instead: "Confirm the signer will attend before you schedule the next call."

Each one is derived from an Echo — a behavior that has repeated across that rep's conversations — not from a single call, and not from a generic playbook.

Generic AI coaching

✕ "Ask more discovery questions"

✕ Derived from one transcript, in isolation

✕ Five suggestions, no ranking

✕ No evidence a rep can check

✕ Nobody ever finds out whether it worked

A Bylda Directive

✓ "Establish decision criteria before quoting"

✓ Derived from a pattern across 18 conversations

✓ One directive, chosen because it repeats

✓ Timestamps the rep can go and listen to

✓ Checked against the outcomes that followed

The part that matters

## A directive that stops working stops being given.

This is the difference between coaching software and a coaching opinion. Because Bylda sees the behavior, the change, and the outcome that followed, it can tell whether the advice it gave was any good.

01

Echo

A behavior that has repeated across this rep's conversations.

02

Directive

One specific change, with the evidence for it attached.

03

Outcome

What happened on the calls after the change.

04

Revision

Directives that do not move outcomes here get retired.

05

Your playbook

What is left is what works in your company, with your buyers.

Over time this is what a Behavior Graph is for. Not a generic methodology bought from a consultancy, but an account of how selling actually works in your market — assembled from your own conversations.

Managers

## Coach the pattern, not the anecdote.

One coaching priority a week for the whole team, chosen because it repeats across reps rather than because you happened to hear it.

Reps

## Coaching every day, not every quarter.

Your own audit, waiting at 7am: what you did well, what cost you, and the one thing to practice today.

Bylda for sales reps →

FAQ

## AI sales coaching, answered.

What is AI sales coaching? +

Software that analyzes a rep's actual conversations and tells them what to change, rather than a manager doing it from memory on whichever calls they had time to hear. The useful version is specific and evidence-backed: one action, derived from a behavior that repeats across that rep's calls, with the timestamps that justify it.

Can AI replace a sales manager? +

No, and it should not try. A manager's judgment about a person, a territory, and a career is not a pattern-matching problem. What AI removes is the part managers cannot do at scale anyway — noticing which behaviors repeat across three hundred conversations a week. The manager still decides what to do about it.

How is this different from a coaching scorecard? +

A scorecard rates a call against a rubric someone wrote in advance. It cannot tell you whether the rubric is right for your market. Bylda works the other way around: it observes what actually differentiates outcomes in your organization, and the directives follow from that evidence rather than from a template.

Why only one directive at a time? +

Because behavior change has a throughput limit. A rep handed five things to fix will fix none of them, and the attempt usually makes the next call worse. Ranking is the product decision that makes coaching actually land.

## Coach what is actually happening.

Bylda finds the pattern in your team's conversations, then tells each rep the one thing to change.

## Sales Performance Analytics With Behavioral Metrics | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/sales-performance-analytics

Sales Performance Analytics

# Analytics that explain the gap.

Every sales org can see that one rep closes at twice the rate of another. Almost none can say what that rep does differently. Bylda measures the behavior, so performance analytics finally have a cause in them.

Request access →

For managers

## The problem with activity analytics

Open any sales analytics tool and you will find calls made, meetings booked, emails sent, pipeline created, stage conversion, deal velocity, win rate. All real, all measured accurately, and all describing volume rather than conduct.

This is why activity dashboards so often produce the same two conclusions: do more, or do it faster. Neither helps the rep who is already making enough calls and losing them, because the variable that matters is not how many conversations happened but what happened inside them.

Activity analytics can tell you a rep is busy. They cannot tell you a rep is quoting before qualifying.

## Behavioral metrics, and what they are for

Bylda adds a layer of measurement that describes conduct across the team and tracks how it moves:

Discovery depth and duration — how much qualifying actually happens, and where it dropped.

Sequence integrity — how often price precedes criteria, or a demo precedes qualification.

Objection handling — response latency and what follows it, by rep and by objection type.

Conversational control — listening ratio, interruptions, where control shifts.

Stakeholder coverage — whether the signer has ever attended, drawn from call rosters rather than CRM contact roles.

Framework execution — whether the methodology you bought is actually being run.

Call duration patterns — the lengths that precede progression, and the ones that precede silence.

These are not vanity metrics because each one names a specific, changeable behavior. A win-rate number tells a manager to worry. A sequence-integrity number tells them what to coach on Monday.

Revenue leaks

## Losses have a location.

A pipeline report can tell you revenue leaked. It cannot point at the moment. Behavioral analytics can, because the leak happened in a conversation that was recorded.

Price quoted before decision criteria established

→ WHERE

Concentrated in one lead source

Signer never attended a call

→ WHERE

Most stalled opportunities

Objection answered in under two seconds

→ WHERE

Four reps, all mid-tenure

Demo delivered before qualification

→ WHERE

Inbound demo requests

Illustrative. Bylda reports the patterns present in your own conversations and says so when a pattern is still too thin to act on.

## What top performers actually do

The most valuable output of behavioral analytics is also the simplest: an explicit description of what your strongest reps do that the others don't. Right now that knowledge lives in one person's head, leaves when they leave, and gets approximated badly in onboarding.

Measured across enough conversations, it becomes teachable — and testable, because the Behavior Graph records whether reps who adopted the behavior actually saw different outcomes.

## It works alongside what you already report

Bylda does not replace your CRM reporting or your BI stack, and it is not trying to become the place you check quota attainment. It supplies the behavioral dimension those systems have never had — and, on the roadmap, writes behavioral context back into the CRM so your existing reports get better inputs.

FAQ

## Sales performance analytics, answered.

What is the difference between activity metrics and behavioral metrics? +

Activity metrics count events: calls made, meetings booked, stages advanced. Behavioral metrics describe conduct: how much discovery happened before the pitch, how quickly an objection was answered, whether the signer attended, how control shifted during the conversation. Activity tells you volume; behavior tells you cause.

How do you measure sales behavior? +

From the conversations themselves. Question count and type per speaker, discovery duration and coverage, interruptions, listening ratio, speaking pace, response latency after objections, the order in which pricing and criteria appear, attendance, and commitment or resistance language. Each is an observable fact about a recording rather than an inference about a person.

How do you find revenue leaks in sales conversations? +

Look for behaviors that recur specifically in conversations that did not progress, then check where they concentrate — a lead source, a tenure band, a deal size, a segment. Concentration is what turns an observation into something actionable, because it tells you whether to fix a rep, a process step, or an intake channel.

Does this replace our BI or CRM reporting? +

No. Bylda adds the behavioral dimension those systems never had and, on the roadmap, writes behavioral context back into the CRM so existing reports get better inputs. Quota attainment and pipeline reporting stay where they are.

## The Bylda Behavior Graph — Behavior Linked to Outcomes

Source: https://usebylda.com/behavior-graph

The Behavior Graph

# Your sales intelligence learns how your team wins.

Analyzing a call is table stakes. The hard part is connecting a behavior to the action a rep took and the outcome that followed — thousands of times, inside one company — until you know which behaviors actually produce revenue here.

Request access →

The category

Concept The behavioral outcome graph is direction only, not product today. What ships now is the loop it will be built on: events, behaviors, patterns and outcomes, each shown with its sample size and confidence. See the vision .

## Why "we use AI" is not a moat

We should say this plainly, because it is the question a serious buyer asks third: the models underneath every product in this category are broadly available, improving fast, and converging. Nobody's advantage is the model. Anyone claiming otherwise is describing a temporary gap.

What does not commoditize is a specific, accumulated record of behavior → action → outcome inside one organization. That data does not exist anywhere else, cannot be bought, and gets more valuable the longer it runs.

The moat is not the analysis. It is knowing which analysis turned out to be right, here, with these buyers.

## What the Behavior Graph connects

Four things, joined:

Seller behavior — what the rep did, in what order, at what pace.

Buyer behavior — what the other side did in response.

The action taken — the directive given, and whether it was followed.

The outcome — booked, advanced, stalled, won, lost, renewed, churned.

Joined across enough conversations, that structure supports a question no scorecard can answer: when this objection appears, and the seller responds this way, at this point in the process, with this type of buyer — what usually happens next?

The join

## Behavior, and what followed.

Every row is one observed behavior paired with the outcome that actually resolved. Rows accumulate. Patterns emerge from your data, not from a template.

Discovery ran long before pricing came up

→ OUTCOME

Second meeting booked

Pricing objection answered immediately, at length

→ OUTCOME

Deal stalled

Implementation questions asked, signer present

→ OUTCOME

Deal advanced

Criteria confirmed before the demo

→ OUTCOME

Deal won

Follow-up sent without referencing the stated concern

→ OUTCOME

No reply

Rows shown are illustrative. Bylda does not publish ratios or lift figures it has not measured in your organization, and it will tell you when a pattern is still too thin to act on.

## The flywheel, stated honestly

More conversations produce more traces. More traces produce better signal detection. Better signals produce sharper directives. Directives produce outcomes. Outcomes tell the graph which directives were right — which improves the next set of signals.

That loop is real and it compounds. It is also slow at the start, and we would rather say so than imply otherwise. In week one Bylda is a very good auditor. The behavioral advantage specific to your company accrues over quarters, not days.

## What it becomes

Rep-specific — the behaviors that work for this rep, given how they actually sell.

Team-specific — the patterns separating your strongest reps from the rest.

Company-specific — the sequence that works on your buyers, at your price point.

Vertical-specific — eventually, how the answer differs by market.

## What we are not claiming

The Behavior Graph is the architecture Bylda is built on and the intelligence it accumulates for you. It is not a pre-trained oracle of universal sales truth, it does not hold millions of other companies' interactions, and it does not predict individual deal outcomes with certainty. Where the evidence is thin, the product says so. See where Bylda is going for the honest split between what ships today and what does not.

FAQ

## The Behavior Graph, answered.

What is the Bylda Behavior Graph? +

The structure that connects seller behavior, buyer behavior, the action taken, and the outcome that followed — accumulated across your organization's conversations over time. It is what lets Bylda move from describing a call to knowing which behaviors tend to produce revenue in your specific market.

Does Bylda train on my company's data to benefit others? +

No. Your conversations are not used to train shared or third-party models. The Behavior Graph built from your data is yours — that is both a privacy commitment and the reason it is valuable. See our security posture for the contractual detail.

How long before it is useful? +

Auditing is useful immediately — the findings on a single week of conversations do not depend on history. The company-specific behavioral patterns take longer, because they require enough resolved outcomes to distinguish a real pattern from noise. We would rather show you a thin result labelled as thin than a confident number we cannot support.

Can it prove a behavior caused an outcome? +

Careful language matters here. Observed association is not proof of cause, and we do not present it as such. What the graph supports is a well-evidenced claim that a behavior is associated with better or worse outcomes in your data, strong enough to be worth changing and then re-measuring. Controlled comparison is a direction we are working toward, not something we claim today.

## Conversation Intelligence vs Behavioral Intelligence | Bylda

Source: https://usebylda.com/conversation-intelligence

Conversation Intelligence

# Searchable calls are not reviewed calls.

Conversation intelligence made every sales call findable. It did not make them reviewed, because a manager still has to open the recording, form a judgment, and remember to act. Behavioral sales intelligence closes that gap.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

## What conversation intelligence got right

Worth stating plainly, because the category deserves credit. Before it existed, a sales call vanished the moment it ended and the only record was whatever the rep typed afterward. Conversation intelligence made calls recorded, transcribed, searchable, and shareable. That was a genuine advance and it is now the foundation everything else in this space is built on, Bylda included.

## Where it stops

The category's implicit promise was that if you could find the calls, you would review them. In practice the arithmetic prevents it: a manager with eight reps has roughly three hundred conversations a week and time for five.

So searchable calls become a searchable archive nobody searches. The metrics that come with it — talk ratio, longest monologue, question count — are real measurements, but they are reported per call and left for a human to interpret, rank, and turn into a coaching decision. That interpretation step is the actual work, and it is exactly the step that does not scale.

The bottleneck was never finding the call. It was having the hours to understand three hundred of them.

The difference

## Conversation intelligence vs

behavioral sales intelligence.

Two architectures for the same raw input

Conversation intelligence Behavioral sales intelligence

Unit of analysis One call Behavior repeating across calls, reps, and outcomes

Primary output A searchable recording and per-call metrics A ranked finding and the change it implies

Who does the interpreting A manager, per call The system, then a manager decides what to do

Coverage in practice The calls someone had time to open Every conversation, every day

Relationship to outcomes Reported alongside Joined to behavior, and used to test the recommendation

What it gets better at Transcription and search Knowing which behaviors produce revenue in your company

This is a comparison of architectures, not a claim that conversation intelligence products are bad. Several are excellent at what they were designed to do, and many teams run both.

Same call, two readings

## What each one hands you.

Conversation intelligence

· Call recorded, 31:04, transcript available

· Talk ratio: rep 68%, buyer 32%

· Longest monologue: 91 seconds

· "Pricing" mentioned 7 times

· Competitor mentioned: no

· Shared with manager for review

Behavioral sales intelligence

✓ Price landed at 09:12, before any decision criteria were established

✓ The objection was answered in 1.4s, then held for 91s

✓ Buyer question rate went to zero and never recovered

✓ The signer was not on the call — and has not been on any

✓ This sequence appears in 9 of this rep's last 18 conversations

✓ Directive: establish criteria and the signer before quoting

The left column is accurate and requires a person to turn it into a decision. The right column is the decision, with the evidence attached — and a note that it is not a one-off.

Illustrative example — product shown with example data

## Do you need both?

Often not, but it depends on what you use the recorder for. If your team relies on call libraries for onboarding, deal handoffs, or legal recall, keep it — Bylda is not an archive and does not try to be.

If the recorder was bought so managers would review more calls, look honestly at whether that happened. In most organizations the review rate never moved, because the constraint was never discoverability. Bylda can read the recordings your existing platform already produces, so adopting it does not require ripping anything out.

## A note on tone, emotion and sentiment

Many products in this category reduce sentiment to one number per call. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment too, but as a timeline tied to moments you can replay , with a confidence level and the context around each shift, so a person can check a reading rather than take it on trust.

FAQ

## Conversation intelligence, answered.

What is conversation intelligence? +

Software that records, transcribes, and analyzes sales calls so they can be searched, shared, and measured — typically reporting per-call metrics such as talk ratio, monologue length, question count, and keyword mentions. It made calls findable, which was a real advance over a world where a conversation vanished when it ended.

What is the difference between conversation intelligence and behavioral sales intelligence? +

The unit of analysis and the output. Conversation intelligence analyzes one call and hands a human per-call metrics to interpret. Behavioral sales intelligence looks for the behaviors that repeat across many calls, reps, and outcomes, and returns a ranked finding with the specific change it implies — then uses what happened next to test whether that recommendation was right.

Do I need both a call recorder and Bylda? +

It depends what the recorder is for. If your team relies on call libraries for onboarding, handoffs, or recall, keep it — Bylda is not an archive. If it was bought so managers would review more calls, check whether the review rate actually moved. Bylda can read the recordings your existing platform already produces, so adoption does not require removing anything.

Is talk ratio a useful metric? +

Mildly, and it is frequently over-used. Talk ratio tells you distribution but not sequence, and sequence is usually what decided the call — a rep who talks 68% of the time while walking a buyer through implementation after full discovery is doing something very different from one who talks 68% justifying a price nobody asked about yet.

Can call analysis detect buyer sentiment? +

Yes. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment across the call and shows them on the timeline next to what happened. Each reading is tied to the moment it came from, so you can replay it, and carries a confidence level. Treat it as a signal to investigate, not a verdict on a person.

## Deal risk lives in behavior, not in fields

By the time a stalled deal shows up in the pipeline report, it has usually been stalling for weeks. The close date slips last. What slips first is behavior: response times stretch, the champion's replies get shorter, the decision maker stops attending, the same objection surfaces on a third call without ever being resolved.

None of that is in the CRM, because none of it is a field. It's a sequence — and sequences are what Bylda is built to read.

The stages say commit. The conversations say risk. Only one of them is right.

## The signals Bylda watches

Stakeholder behavior — who is in the room, who joined late, who disappeared, and whether the economic buyer has actually engaged.

Objection trajectories — not just that a concern was raised, but whether the response resolved it or papered over it.

Engagement shifts — reply speed, meeting acceptance, forwarding behavior, and when they change.

Seller behavior — the follow-up that led with pricing when the concern was implementation; the discount offered before it was asked for.

Timing — commitments with dates, dates that move, and urgency that rises or quietly drains away.

Each signal is grounded in something that was actually said or done. Nothing is inferred from a stage's age or a rep's optimism — that's the difference between behavioral deal intelligence and a record-based system guessing from its own fields.

FAQ

## Deal intelligence, answered.

What is deal intelligence? +

Software that understands the state of a deal from actual commercial activity — conversations, email, meetings, stakeholder engagement — rather than from the fields a rep filled in. Good deal intelligence answers three questions: what changed, why it matters, and what to do next.

How do you identify a deal at risk before it stalls? +

Stalls announce themselves in behavior before they show up in the pipeline: response times stretch, a champion goes quiet, the decision maker stops attending, an objection gets raised repeatedly without being resolved, or procurement takes over the conversation. Bylda watches for these patterns across every deal and flags the change with its evidence — typically before the close date has moved at all.

What is a next best action in sales? +

A specific, evidence-backed recommendation for what to do on a deal right now — for example, bringing the economic buyer into the conversation before revising pricing. Bylda derives it from the deal's observed behavior, and pairs it with the execution: the drafted follow-up, the created task, the updated CRM.

How is deal intelligence different from a deal score? +

A score is a number without a reason. Deal intelligence is the reason: which behavior changed, what it means for this deal, and what the sensible response is. Bylda shows scores where they help, but every one traces back to specific observed moments a rep can verify.

## Bylda for Sales Managers — Coach Without Reviewing Calls

Source: https://usebylda.com/for-sales-managers

For Sales Managers & Heads of Sales

# Coach the team without listening to every call.

You can review five calls a week. Your team has three hundred. Bylda audits all of them and hands you the short list: who needs help, what is repeating, where revenue is leaking, and what your best reps do differently.

Request access →

See a team audit

## The arithmetic nobody says out loud

Eight reps, six conversations a day each, five days a week. That is roughly three hundred conversations, and a manager with a forecast to run, escalations to handle, and their own pipeline reviews to sit in has time for maybe five of them.

So the sample you coach from is not representative — it is whichever calls happened to be on the calendar when you had a free hour. Whatever is systematically going wrong is, by definition, happening mostly in the calls you never hear.

You are not under-coaching because you lack discipline. You are under-coaching because 300 does not fit into 5.

## What changes when every call is audited

Not more dashboards. A shorter list. Bylda reads every conversation and surfaces only what is both recurring and consequential — then tells you which two reps to start with.

Your Monday

## Five questions, answered before you ask.

Who needs help? Ranked by behavior, not by attainment

Why? The specific conduct, with timestamps

What is repeating? Echoes across multiple reps

Where is revenue leaking? Located in the conversation

What do my best reps do differently? Made explicit, so it can be taught

Then one coaching priority for the week. Not forty metrics with no ranking — the thing most worth an hour of your attention, and the evidence for why.

## Pipeline reviews stop being interrogations

The standard review runs on reconstruction: a rep describes calls from memory, a manager probes for the part being left out, and an hour disappears before anyone makes a decision. When every conversation has already been audited, the room starts at the decision instead.

## The thing managers worry about, addressed

Auditing every call can become surveillance, and that would make your team worse, not better. We have made deliberate product choices against it: the rep sees their own audit before you do, findings describe conduct rather than character, strengths are reported alongside leaks, and there is no leaderboard anywhere in the product.

The test we hold ourselves to is whether a rep would open Bylda voluntarily. A tool your team resents produces gamed behavior and worse data — which defeats the entire point.

FAQ

## For managers, answered.

How can a sales manager review more calls? +

They mostly can't, and that is the wrong goal. The number of calls a manager can listen to is fixed by the hours in a week. What scales is changing what gets reviewed: instead of recordings, review findings — a short ranked list of behaviors that repeat across the team, each linked to the timestamp that evidences it.

What should I coach first? +

Whatever repeats across multiple reps, because that is a system problem rather than an individual one and fixing it compounds. One rep's habit is worth a conversation; the same habit on four reps is an enablement gap, a hiring profile, or a broken step in your sales process.

Will my reps feel monitored? +

It depends on how the tool behaves, which is why Bylda is designed rep-first: they see their own audit before their manager does, findings are about conduct rather than character, strengths appear alongside leaks, and there is no leaderboard. How you introduce it matters as much as the product — we will help with that.

Does this replace my sales methodology? +

No. Bylda can measure whether your methodology is actually being executed — which most organizations cannot currently see — and over time show you which parts of it correlate with outcomes in your market. That tends to strengthen a methodology rather than replace it.

## Most reps are coached almost never

The honest version of sales coaching in most organizations: a few sessions a quarter, based on whichever call your manager happened to sit in on, delivered as general advice you have heard before. Everything else is you guessing about your own habits — which is impossible, because you cannot hear yourself the way a buyer does.

The information you need already exists. It is in your own calls. Nobody has the hours to go and find it.

You are not missing effort. You are missing a mirror.

## The leak is almost always a sequence, not a skill.

Reps expect to be told they need to be more persuasive. Far more often, the finding is about order and timing.

Price arriving before decision criteria. An objection answered in a second and a half, at length, instead of with a question. A demo given before anyone confirmed what they were evaluating. None of these are character flaws. They are habits, they are visible in the recording, and they are genuinely fixable in a week.

Your patterns measured against your own outcomes, not a team average

Evidence you can verify — every claim has a timestamp

No leaderboard, no ranking, no talk-ratio shaming

You see your audit before your manager does

FAQ

## For reps, answered.

Is this a tool for my manager to monitor me? +

You see your own audit first. Findings describe conduct, with a timestamp you can check, rather than rating you as a person. Strengths are reported alongside leaks. There is no leaderboard. If reps do not open it voluntarily, we have built the wrong product — that is the standard we hold it to.

What if I disagree with a finding? +

Go and listen to the timestamp. Every claim Bylda makes points at a specific moment precisely so you can check it, and sometimes you will be right and it will be wrong. A finding you cannot verify is not evidence, it is an assertion — which is why the product is built to cite rather than to score.

Do I have to do anything during calls? +

No. No bot to invite, no button to remember, no notes to take. Bylda works from the recordings and activity your stack already produces, and the audit is waiting when you start the day.

Will it tell me to sound like everyone else? +

It should not, and that is a design position, not an accident. Bylda measures your patterns against your own outcomes — what works when you do it. Two strong reps often win in opposite ways, and a product that flattens that difference would be destroying the thing it is supposed to find.

## Why this page isn't testimonials

Most early-stage sales tools put three case studies and eight logos on a page like this. You have read those pages. You know roughly how much of it to believe, and you have probably learned to skim past them to the pricing.

We would rather spend the page on something you can actually use: whether this is going to work for your team. If it isn't, finding that out here saves us both a call.

When we have customers willing to be named, they will be named, with numbers they agreed to. Until then, this page stays honest.

Fit

## Where Bylda works,

and where it doesn't.

A good fit

✓ B2B sales teams of roughly 5–150 reps

✓ Calls are already recorded — Zoom, Meet, Teams, or a dialer

✓ A CRM is in use, even if the data in it is poor

✓ Managers have more reps than listening hours

✓ Deals involve discovery, objections, and more than one stakeholder

✓ Someone can name a performance gap they cannot currently explain

Not a fit yet

✕ Sales happens mostly over email or chat, not conversation

✕ Calls are not recorded and cannot be, for policy or legal reasons

✕ Transactional selling with little discovery — one call, one close

✕ Fewer than about five reps, where a manager genuinely hears everything

✕ You want a call recorder or a CRM — Bylda is neither

✕ You want guaranteed win-rate lift in writing. Nobody can honestly offer that

If you are in the right column, we will tell you on the first call rather than sell you a pilot that disappoints.

The evaluation

## One week of real calls. That's the whole test.

No six-week pilot, no success criteria workshop. Either the findings are ones you would have reached yourself with unlimited listening time, or they aren't.

DAY 1

Connect

OAuth to your conferencing, calendar, and CRM. Scoped, reviewed, reversible.

DAY 2

First audits

Bylda reads the conversations that already happened. Nothing to schedule.

WEEK 1

Echoes appear

Behaviors repeating across reps start separating from one-offs.

THE TEST

Verify one

Pick a finding you doubt. Listen to the timestamp. Decide if it is right.

THEN

Your call

If the findings are not useful, say so and we stop. No pilot to unwind.

The verification step is the one that matters. Every claim Bylda makes points at a moment you can check, which means you are never asked to trust the software — only to audit it once.

## What we will and won't claim

Since this page exists in place of results, it should be clear about the difference between the two.

We will say what Bylda observed in your conversations, with the timestamp behind it, and whether a pattern is strong enough to act on or still too thin.

We will say which behaviors are associated with better outcomes in your own data, once enough outcomes have resolved to tell signal from noise.

We will not say that a behavior caused an outcome. Observed association is not proof of cause, and anyone selling you certainty on that is selling something else.

We will not say a number like "31% more meetings" unless it came from your data and we can show the working.

We will not invent a customer, a quote, or a logo. Which is why this page reads the way it does.

The same principle runs through the product: see what ships today versus what doesn't , and how the Behavior Graph accrues rather than arriving pre-trained.

## Who you'll be talking to

Early access is small on purpose. You will work directly with the people building the product, the feedback loop is days rather than quarters, and the behavioral patterns we find in your market shape what gets built next. That is the actual trade in an early-access program, and it is worth more than a discount.

Questions

Does Bylda have customers yet? +

Bylda is in early access and works with a small number of design-partner teams. Rather than publish case studies before there are customers willing to be named with numbers they agreed to, the site states what the product fits and what an evaluation involves.

What kind of sales team is Bylda a good fit for? +

B2B teams of roughly 5 to 150 reps, where calls are already recorded, a CRM is in use, managers have more reps than listening hours, and deals involve discovery, objections, and more than one stakeholder.

When is Bylda not a fit? +

When selling happens mostly over email or chat rather than conversation, when calls cannot be recorded for policy or legal reasons, in transactional one-call closes with little discovery, or on teams small enough that a manager genuinely hears every call.

What does an evaluation involve? +

Connect over OAuth, let Bylda read a week of conversations that already happened, then verify a finding you doubt by listening to the timestamp it cites. There is no lengthy pilot to unwind if the findings are not useful.

## Bylda vs Gong — An Architectural Comparison

Source: https://usebylda.com/gong-alternative

Comparison

# Bylda vs Gong

Two products that read the same recordings and do fundamentally different things with them. This page explains the architectural difference honestly, including where Gong is the better choice.

Request access →

See a Phantom Audit

## The short version

Gong is a revenue intelligence platform built on conversation capture. It records, transcribes, and makes calls searchable, reports metrics about them, and layers deal and forecast intelligence on top. It is a large, mature product and it is good at what it was designed to do.

Bylda is a behavioral sales intelligence platform. It analyzes the conduct inside conversations, finds the behaviors that repeat across a team, and returns one specific change per person with the evidence — then checks that recommendation against what happened next.

Gong gives you the calls and the numbers about them. Bylda gives you the finding and what to do about it.

If you want a searchable library of every customer conversation, Gong does that and Bylda does not. If your problem is that nobody has the hours to review the library you already have, that is the problem Bylda was built for.

The difference

## Different unit. Different output.

Architectural comparison. Product capabilities change — verify current details with each vendor.

Gong Bylda

Category Revenue intelligence, built on conversation capture Behavioral sales intelligence

Unit of analysis The call, and pipeline aggregates Behavior repeating across calls, reps, and outcomes

Primary output Searchable recordings, per-call metrics, deal and forecast views A ranked finding and one directive, with its evidence

Who interprets A manager, per call or per dashboard The system ranks; the manager decides what to do

Call library Yes — a core strength No. Bylda is not an archive

Coaching model Scorecards and manager review of selected calls One directive per rep, derived from a repeated pattern

Recommendation testing Not the design goal Outcomes are used to judge whether a directive worked

Emotion / sentiment Sentiment features are marketed Scored on the call timeline, tied to replayable moments, with confidence stated

Maturity Large, mature, widely deployed Early access. Small, and honest about it

We describe Gong from its public product documentation and marketing. We do not publish benchmark claims against it, and we would treat anyone who did with suspicion.

Honest split

## When to pick which.

Gong is the better choice when

· You need a searchable library of every customer conversation

· Call recordings matter for onboarding, handoffs, or recall

· You want forecasting and pipeline intelligence in the same platform

· Procurement requires a large, established vendor

· Your managers genuinely do review calls and want better tooling for it

Bylda is the better choice when

✓ You bought a recorder and the review rate never actually moved

✓ You need to know what repeats across reps, not what happened on one call

✓ You want a specific change per rep, not a scorecard

✓ You care whether the coaching advice was right, measured against outcomes

✓ You want sentiment and emotion tied to moments you can replay, not a bare score

These are not mutually exclusive. Bylda can read the recordings your existing platform already produces, so running both is a normal configuration rather than a migration.

## The question worth asking your own team

Before comparing feature lists, check one number: how many calls did your managers actually review last month, and out of how many?

For most organizations the ratio is somewhere under five percent, and it has not changed since the recorder was installed. That is not a criticism of the recorder — discoverability was a genuine problem and it got solved. It just means the remaining bottleneck is the reviewing, and no amount of better search fixes an hours problem.

If your ratio is high and your managers are getting what they need, you do not have the problem Bylda solves. If it is under five percent, the interesting question is what is in the other ninety-five. That is the case for auditing every conversation rather than sampling.

## On switching

Usually you don't have to. Bylda reads from conferencing platforms and can work alongside an existing recorder rather than replacing it, so evaluating us does not require unwinding a contract or retraining a team. If you do eventually consolidate, that is a decision to make with evidence in hand, not before.

FAQ

## Bylda vs Gong, answered.

Is Bylda a Gong alternative? +

For the coaching and call-review job, yes. For the call-library job, no — Bylda is not an archive and does not try to be. Many teams run both: Bylda can read the recordings an existing platform already produces.

What does Bylda do that Gong doesn't? +

Three things structurally. It treats behavior repeating across many calls as the unit of analysis rather than the individual call. It returns one ranked directive per person rather than metrics to interpret. And it uses the outcomes that follow to judge whether its own recommendation was right — a directive that stops working stops being given.

What does Gong do that Bylda doesn't? +

A searchable call library, forecasting and pipeline intelligence in the same platform, and the maturity of a large deployed product. Gong is also a far safer procurement decision today — we are in early access and would rather say so than pretend otherwise.

Do I have to replace my call recorder? +

No. Bylda can read recordings your existing platform produces, so an evaluation does not require unwinding a contract or retraining anyone.

Does Bylda do sentiment analysis like other call platforms? +

Yes. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment, shown on the call timeline next to what happened. The difference is that every reading points to a moment you can replay and carries a confidence level, so it is a signal you can check, not a single score to trust.

## Find out what's in the other ninety-five percent.

Bylda reads the recordings you already have. One week is enough.

## Bylda vs Clari — Forecasting vs Behavioral Intelligence

Source: https://usebylda.com/clari-alternative

Comparison

# Bylda vs Clari

These two products work at opposite ends of the same problem. Clari aggregates what the pipeline says. Bylda measures what happened in the conversations that produced it. Most teams eventually need both.

Request access →

The category

## Not really competitors

Clari is a revenue operations and forecasting platform. It pulls together pipeline data, applies models to it, and gives leadership a view of the number — commit, best case, risk, and how those move week to week. It is genuinely good at that, and if forecasting is your problem, Bylda does not solve it.

Bylda works upstream of the data Clari consumes. It reads the conversations, measures the conduct inside them, and tells a manager which behaviors are moving revenue. It produces explanation and coaching, not a forecast.

Clari tells you the number is going to miss. Bylda tells you which behaviors are making it miss, while there is still time.

The difference

## Aggregate versus cause.

Architectural comparison. Product capabilities change — verify current details with each vendor.

Clari Bylda

Category Revenue operations and forecasting Behavioral sales intelligence

Input CRM records and pipeline activity Sales conversations, plus CRM context

Question answered What will we close, and what is at risk? Which behaviors are producing or costing revenue?

Primary user Revenue leadership and RevOps Sales managers and reps

Output Forecast, roll-ups, risk views A ranked finding and one directive, with evidence

Accuracy ceiling Bounded by what was entered into the CRM Bounded by what was said in the conversation

Forecasting Yes — the core product No. Bylda does not forecast

Coaching Not the design goal The design goal

We describe Clari from its public product documentation. We publish no benchmark claims against it.

The shared dependency

## Both are only as good as the layer beneath.

A forecasting platform inherits its inputs. If the stage was set by a rep from memory, the close date defaults to quarter-end, and the loss reason says "price" because "price" is the first item in the picklist, then the model is forecasting the CRM rather than the business.

This is not a criticism of forecasting tools — it is arithmetic. No modelling technique recovers information that was never captured, and CRM error is directional rather than random: records get updated most diligently when deals are going well.

Bylda works on that layer. It writes record context from what actually happened and measures the conduct underneath, which means the aggregate a forecasting platform consumes is finally describing something real. The two are complementary in a specific, mechanical way: forecast error is inherited, not modeled .

## Which to buy first

Depends on whose problem is louder.

Buy forecasting first if leadership cannot see the number, board reporting is painful, and the pipeline data is broadly trusted. That is a visibility problem at the top.

Buy behavioral intelligence first if you can see the number fine and cannot explain it — reps at wildly different attainment on similar activity, losses attributed to "price," and managers with no capacity to review calls. That is a causation problem in the middle.

One honest tell: if your forecast is accurate but your win rate is flat, forecasting is not your constraint. You already know what will happen — you just cannot change it.

## Running both

They do not conflict. Bylda reads conversations and writes behavioral context into the CRM; a forecasting platform reads the CRM. There is no overlap to reconcile and no migration in either direction.

FAQ

## Bylda vs Clari, answered.

Is Bylda a Clari alternative? +

Not really — they answer different questions. Clari forecasts and aggregates pipeline; Bylda explains behavior inside conversations and coaches on it. If you need a forecast, Bylda does not provide one.

Does Bylda forecast revenue? +

No. Bylda measures behavior and its association with outcomes; it does not produce a commit number or a pipeline roll-up. It improves the inputs a forecasting platform consumes, which is a different contribution.

Which should we buy first? +

If leadership cannot see the number, buy forecasting. If you can see the number and cannot explain it — reps at different attainment on similar activity, losses attributed to price, managers with no capacity to review calls — buy behavioral intelligence. An accurate forecast alongside a flat win rate is a strong sign that forecasting is not the constraint.

Can we run Bylda and a forecasting platform together? +

Yes, and it is the common configuration. Bylda reads conversations and writes behavioral context into the CRM; the forecasting platform reads the CRM. No overlap, no migration.

## Know the number. Then know why.

Bylda works on the layer your forecast is built from.

Is there a minimum seat count? +

Five seats on Core and Team. Enterprise starts at fifty. We would rather you roll out to a full pod than sprinkle single seats across a team — the intelligence compounds when a whole book of business is covered.

Do you charge per minute of recording? +

No. Call analysis is unlimited on every plan. A rep having more customer conversations is the entire point — we are not going to bill you for it.

How long does implementation take? +

Connect the place your calls already live (your CRM, dialer or recorder) or upload recordings, and you are live. Most teams finish in an afternoon. There is no data migration, because Bylda works alongside the CRM you already have.

## FAQ — How Bylda Works, Pricing, CRMs and Data

Source: https://usebylda.com/faq

FAQ

# Everything, answered plainly.

Including the questions with awkward answers.

What is Bylda? +

Bylda is behavioral sales intelligence software. It turns recorded sales calls and CRM activity into behaviors, patterns and outcomes, gives each rep one change to make, and measures whether the behavior changed. It sits alongside the CRM, dialer and call recorder you already use rather than replacing them.

How is this different from a CRM? +

A CRM records activity and stores what someone typed after the fact. Bylda measures the conduct inside the conversations that produced those records — how much discovery happened, how objections were handled, where pricing landed relative to decision criteria, who actually attended. Your CRM stays the system of record; Bylda is the system of intelligence on top of it.

How is this different from Gong or conversation intelligence? +

Conversation intelligence analyzes one call at a time and hands a human per-call metrics to interpret. Bylda treats behavior repeating across many calls, reps and outcomes as the unit of analysis, returns one ranked directive with the evidence behind it, and then uses what happened next to judge whether that recommendation was right. Bylda is not a call library, so many teams run both.

Does it work with our CRM? +

Bylda reads calls and activity from your CRM, dialer or call recorder, or from a manual upload. Salesforce and HubSpot are the two we document in detail. Writing behavioral context back into the CRM is on the roadmap, not in the first release. If you run something else, ask us.

Do reps have to change how they work? +

No. That is the point. Reps get a 60-second brief with one focus, and their own calls and progress. There is nothing to switch on during a call, because Bylda reads the recordings your tools already make.

How long does implementation take? +

Most teams are live in an afternoon. Point Bylda at where your calls already live (your CRM, dialer or recorder) or upload recordings. There is no data migration because Bylda works alongside the CRM you already have.

What if our CRM data is a mess? +

That is the normal starting condition and it is not a blocker — Bylda reads conversations, not your existing records, so poor CRM data does not degrade the analysis. We will show you the change against your own baseline rather than quote a completeness figure from someone else’s deployment.

Does Bylda score tone, emotion, or sentiment? +

Yes. Bylda scores tone, emotion and sentiment alongside conduct such as questions asked, pauses, interruptions, response latency, speaking pace, sequence and attendance. Each reading appears on the call timeline, tied to the moment it came from, with a confidence level, so it can be checked by listening. They are signals to investigate, not verdicts on a person.

Is our conversation data used to train AI models? +

Never. Your conversations are not used to train shared or third-party models.

What does it cost? +

Core is $89 per rep per month and Team is $129, both billed monthly with 20% off annually. Enterprise is custom. Call analysis is unlimited on every plan.

Can we trial it before committing? +

Yes. Bring one week of your team's real conversations. Pick a finding you doubt, listen to the timestamp Bylda cites, and decide whether it is right. If the findings are not useful, we stop — there is no long pilot to unwind. You keep everything Bylda produced either way.

How does Bylda handle recording consent and data protection? +

Bylda analyzes recordings your team already makes, so recording consent stays with the tool that records. How Bylda handles and protects that data, including the DPA, is on the security page. If you need something specific, ask us.
